prompt:
I need the front end for Nightshift. A lab-built tool a university visual computing group uses to keep watch over long overnight rendering jobs on the department's shared compute cluster and get alerted when something goes wrong.

Who's using it: Yuto Hasegawa, 27, a fourth-year PhD student in a graphics research lab. He is producing the supplementary video for the lab's paper on a new subsurface scattering method. He is fluent with the cluster and the renderer, but tired, and he wants to sleep instead of checking jobs every hour.

What they're doing right now: It's 11:30 pm Friday. He has just queued the final renders for all six shots of the video, which is due with the conference submission in 18 days. He wants to know only when it really matters: if a node dies, if frames come back black or full of bright speckle artifacts, or if a shot falls so far behind that it won't finish by Sunday when his advisor wants to review a cut. Right now he is going through how the jobs are progressing and deciding which conditions should wake him up and which can wait until morning.

What's in the system at this point: There are 6 shots ('marble_bust_turntable' 1–360, 'skin_closeup' 1–240, 'jade_dragon' 1–300, 'milk_pour' 1–180, 'comparison_split' 1–240, 'teaser' 1–120), 1,440 frames in all at 1920×1080 and 4,096 samples per pixel. 22 of the cluster's 32 GPU nodes are allocated to the lab, and nodes gpu-17 and gpu-23 show intermittent errors. So far 386 frames are done, 41 are rendering, 1,004 are queued, and 9 failed (7 out-of-memory on 'milk_pour', 2 node timeouts). Average frame time ranges from 3 m 40 s ('teaser') to 22 m ('milk_pour'). Automated frame checks have flagged 3 frames with mean luminance near zero and 5 with outlier pixel counts above threshold. The lab's fair-share quota resets Monday 00:00. The estimated finish time for all shots is Sunday 14:10, with 'milk_pour' trailing to Monday 03:00. Other lab members' jobs are also running.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
